cards.question: A loop has a battery and three bulbs in series. Where is the current smallest?
options: Nowhere: it's the same all the way round
cards.why: In a single loop the current is the same at every point. The bulbs take energy from it, not current.

cards.question: Why does a lamp light the instant you close the switch, though electrons drift less than a millimetre a second?
options: The wire is already full of charge, and the push travels almost at the speed of light
The battery fires electrons down the wire very fast
The lamp stores charge from last time
cards.why: Every electron in the loop starts drifting at once, because the push travels round the whole loop almost instantly.

cards.question: What does "5 V at this point" mean on a schematic?
cards.why: Voltage is always between two points. A voltage given at one point is measured from ground.

cards.question: Your meter is in amps mode and you touch the probes across a lamp. What happens?
options: It shorts the lamp out and probably blows the meter's fuse
cards.why: In amps mode a meter is nearly a plain wire. To read current it has to go in a break in the loop.

cards.question: You need 12 V to push 25 mA through a resistor. Which do you fit?
cards.why: R = V ÷ I = 12 ÷ 0.025 = 480 Ω, and 470 Ω is the nearest standard value.

cards.question: Why do filament bulbs usually fail just as they're switched on?
options: A cold filament has low resistance, so it takes a surge of current
The voltage is higher at switch-on
cards.why: Cold tungsten resists about a tenth as much as hot, so for an instant the current is several times normal.
